title: One repository, many agents
dek: A git checkout is single-occupancy: one HEAD, one index, one set of files. Worktrees split those three off and share everything else, which is why they are the cheap way to run several agents on one repository. This guide reads git worktrees from git@v2.55.0, measures them against five other ways to get a second checkout, and tries to make concurrent agents collide.
byline: 21 October 2026 · Subject: git@e9019fca (v2.55.0) · Read from the source and the manual; measured on this machine
description: How git worktrees work, read from the git 2.55 source: what is shared, what is private, the one-branch rule, prune, sparse checkout, partial clone, and measured costs for running many agents on one repo.
og_description: Git worktrees read from git v2.55.0: the shared/private split in path.c, what git worktree add writes, why a branch can be checked out once, how gc protects every worktree's index, when prune deletes, and what a second checkout costs measured six ways. Plus concurrency probes: 400 commits and 120 fetches from parallel worktrees, zero lock failures.
twitter_description: Git worktrees from the source and a lab: what is shared, what is private, and what a second checkout costs for parallel agents.

from the code marks a fact read from git at e9019fca (tag v2.55.0, 29 June 2026), cited as a path and line number from the repository root; the manual pages are cited under Documentation/. measured here marks a number or behaviour observed with git version 2.55.0 on a 2-vCPU Linux box, on a clone of git.git itself (4,765 tracked files, a 320 MiB pack). Timings are medians of three runs; differences under about 20% are noise. reconstruction marks a judgement I drew from those sources rather than read in one place.
